Thurgau
TOOR-gow
n. (the Swiss common lordship where the Peace of Kappel left Reformed and Catholic sharing the same parish churches)
German Thurgau, the district of the river Thur; a common lordship of the Swiss cantons before it became a canton in 1803.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thurgau is where the Swiss Reformation's stalemate was written into the furniture of the churches. It was not a canton but a common lordship, governed jointly by seven or eight cantons which after 1531 were divided between the Reformed and the Catholic sides, and neither bloc could impose its religion on a territory the other half-owned. The Second Peace of Kappel, concluded in November 1531 after Zwingli's death in the field, settled the common lordships by parity: each parish kept whatever it then had, Catholic worship was restored where it had been abolished, and in a large number of Thurgau parishes both communions were to use the same building, the Reformed holding the nave and the Catholics keeping the choir, often with a screen or rail between and the two services at different hours. Many of these shared churches are still shared. The dictionary enters Thurgau because the arrangement is the plainest monument in Europe to a reformation that was stopped short, and because the people in those parishes had to live as neighbours with men they believed to be in grave error, and mostly did.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines parity as equality; a nave as the body of a church; a choir as the part of a church where the singers sit; and a lordship as the territory of a lord.

expand to see more

PARITY, n. Equality; as a parity of reasoning; equality of condition or of rank.

NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balluster or railing of the door to the chief choir.

CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers.

LORDSHIP, n. The state or quality of being a lord; the seigniory or domain of a lord.

PARTITION, n. That by which separate parts are made; a wall or division which separates one part from another.

Key Scripture

Rom 12:18 — "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

Rom 14:5 — "One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind."

Rom 14:19 — "Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another."

Mat 5:9 — "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Modern Corruption

Swiss common lordship where the Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 established parity, leaving many parishes with Reformed and Catholic worship in one shared church.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the pretence that such a settlement is agreement. Parity in Thurgau was not an ecumenical achievement but a truce between cantons that had just fought a war and could not win another, and the dictionary does not call a shared roof a shared faith; the two services taught contrary doctrines of the mass in the same building on the same morning. What can be said for it is that it stopped the killing and left the preaching free on both sides of the screen, and “live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) is an apostolic command that a truce can serve.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the pursuit of peace is a positive duty and not merely the absence of a quarrel: “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19). The dictionary applies the apostle's word about the esteeming of days in its own place, that “every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5), to the manner of living alongside a neighbour in error, and not to the error itself. Over four centuries of Thurgau parishioners who managed it, the word stands: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eireneuo (G1514), to live in peace; Greek dioko (G1377), to follow after, to pursue; Greek plerophoreo (G4135), to be fully persuaded.

expand to see more

Greek eireneuo (G1514) — to be at peace, to live peaceably; “live peaceably with all men”, Romans 12:18.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to follow hard after; “follow after the things which make for peace”, Romans 14:19.

Greek oikodome (G3619) — a building up, edification; “things wherewith one may edify another”, Romans 14:19.

Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to be fully convinced; “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind”, Romans 14:5.

Greek eirenopoios (G1518) — a peacemaker; “Blessed are the peacemakers”, Matthew 5:9.

Usage

"“live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) — the Second Peace of Kappel, November 1531."

"“follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19) — the nave Reformed and the choir Catholic in one building."

"“Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9) — shared parish churches still shared after four centuries."
